chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Global Central Banks India Watches

lessons.title: QE and Quantitative Tightening: Printing Money and Pulling It Back

body.text: When interest rates hit zero, central banks found a second lever: buying bonds with newly created money, known as quantitative easing. Reversing it, quantitative tightening, pulls that money back out. The size of the Fed's balance sheet has become a force in its own right, pumping liquidity into or draining it from markets all over the world, including India's.

children.text: In the last lesson you saw how the Fed's interest rate decisions reach Dalal Street. This lesson covers the Fed's other, less visible tool. It explains how QE and QT work, why "printing money" is only half the story, and how the Fed's balance sheet helped drive India's biggest foreign investment boom and one of its sharpest reversals.
Why QE Was Invented

markDefs.definition: The practical limit on how far a central bank can cut short-term interest rates, since people could simply hold cash rather than accept deeply negative rates.

children.text: Normally, a central bank fights a downturn by cutting its policy rate. But in 2008, and again in 2020, the Fed cut its rate to near zero and the economy still needed help. Rates cannot usefully go much below zero, a limit economists call the
zero lower bound
. With its main tool exhausted, the Fed needed another way to push borrowing costs down.

markDefs.definition: Large-scale purchases of government bonds and other securities by a central bank, paid for with newly created reserves, to lower long-term interest rates and support the economy when policy rates are already near zero.

children.text: The answer was
quantitative easing (QE)
: buying huge amounts of government bonds and mortgage-backed securities, not to manage day-to-day liquidity, but to push long-term interest rates down and flood the financial system with money.
How QE Works, Step by Step
The Fed buys US Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities from banks and investors.
It pays by creating new bank reserves electronically. No physical notes are printed.
Heavy buying pushes bond prices up and long-term yields down, making mortgages and business loans cheaper.
Investors who sold their bonds now hold cash earning little, so they move into riskier assets: stocks, corporate bonds and emerging markets.
Lower US yields tend to weaken the dollar and send money abroad in search of better returns.

markDefs.definition: When central bank bond buying pushes investors out of safe, low-yielding assets into riskier ones like stocks and emerging market assets, lifting their prices.

children.text: Step 4 has a name: the
portfolio rebalancing effect
. It is the main reason QE lifts asset prices far beyond the US bond market.

body.text: "Printing money" is a useful shorthand, but not quite accurate. QE creates bank reserves held at the Fed, not cash in people's wallets. That is why QE after 2008 did not cause high US inflation for a decade: much of the new money stayed inside the banking system and financial markets, pushing up asset prices rather than consumer prices. Pandemic-era QE was different because it came alongside huge government spending that put money directly in households' hands.

body.title: Name the Policy
body.textWithBlank: When a central bank buys bonds with newly created reserves to lower long-term interest rates, it is using quantitative ___.
body.explanation: Quantitative easing, or QE. The opposite, shrinking the balance sheet by letting bonds mature or selling them, is quantitative tightening, or QT.

body.title: US Federal Reserve Total Assets ($ trillion)
Fifteen Years of QE and QT

events.title: QE1 begins
events.description: After the Lehman Brothers collapse, the Fed starts buying mortgage-backed securities and Treasuries to stabilise markets.

events.title: QE2
events.description: The Fed announces $600 billion of longer-term Treasury purchases, about $75 billion a month.

events.title: QE3
events.description: An open-ended programme, eventually buying about $85 billion a month of Treasuries and mortgage securities.

events.title: Balance sheet near $4.5 trillion
events.description: Nearly five times its pre-crisis size after three rounds of QE.

events.title: Pandemic QE
events.description: Starting from about $4.2 trillion, the Fed buys around $3 trillion of securities in roughly three months.

events.title: Peak at $8.96 trillion
events.description: The largest central bank balance sheet in US history.

events.title: QT begins
events.description: The Fed lets up to $95 billion of bonds a month mature without reinvesting: $60 billion of Treasuries and $35 billion of mortgage securities.

events.title: QT ends
events.description: After 41 months, the balance sheet had shrunk to about $6.57 trillion, roughly $2.4 trillion below its peak.

events.title: Reserve management purchases start
events.description: The Fed begins buying Treasury bills, about $40 billion in the first round, to keep bank reserves ample. This is technical support for money markets, not QE to stimulate the economy.

body.title: How Big Was Pandemic QE?
body.prompt: The Fed's balance sheet was about $4.2 trillion in March 2020 and peaked at $8.96 trillion in April 2022. By what percentage did it grow? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ($8.96 trillion − $4.2 trillion) ÷ $4.2 trillion × 100 = 113.3%. The balance sheet more than doubled in about two years. For comparison, it took the Fed six years, from 2008 to 2014, to grow from $0.9 trillion to $4.5 trillion.

body.title: How Much Did QT Undo?
body.prompt: The balance sheet grew from $4.2 trillion to $8.96 trillion during the pandemic, then shrank to $6.57 trillion when QT ended. What percentage of the pandemic expansion did QT reverse? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Pandemic expansion = $8.96 trillion − $4.2 trillion = $4.76 trillion. Reduction during QT = $8.96 trillion − $6.57 trillion = $2.39 trillion. Share reversed = $2.39 trillion ÷ $4.76 trillion × 100 = 50.2%. Only about half. The Fed stopped QT because shrinking reserves too far risked disrupting US money markets, a reminder that QE is much easier to start than to unwind.

children.text: QE vs QT: Opposite Forces

columns.label: Quantitative easing (QE)
points: Central bank buys bonds and creates reserves
Long-term yields fall
Investors pushed into stocks and riskier assets
Dollar tends to weaken
Money flows into emerging markets like India

columns.label: Quantitative tightening (QT)
points: Central bank lets bonds mature or sells them, reserves shrink
Long-term yields tend to rise
Liquidity for risky assets dries up
Dollar tends to strengthen
Money flows out of emerging markets

children.text: How QE and QT Moved India
The Flood: 2020 and 2021

Pandemic QE, combined with near-zero rates everywhere, sent a wave of money into emerging markets. India, with strong growth prospects, caught more than its share. Foreign portfolio investors poured a record net ₹2.74 lakh crore, about $37.4 billion, into Indian equities in FY21, making India the largest recipient of FPI flows among emerging markets that year.

body.title: Measure the QE-Era Rally
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 rose from 7,511 on 24 March 2020 to 18,604 on 18 October 2021. What was the percentage gain? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (18,604 − 7,511) ÷ 7,511 × 100 = 147.7%. The index rose to nearly two-and-a-half times its crash low in 19 months. QE was not the only reason, since Indian companies' earnings recovered strongly and domestic investors poured money into SIPs, but abundant global liquidity was a powerful tailwind.

children.text: The Ebb: 2022

Then the tide turned. From March 2022 the Fed started hiking rates, and from June 2022 it began QT. Global liquidity shrank, the dollar surged and US yields climbed. Foreign investors pulled a record net ₹1.21 lakh crore out of Indian equities in calendar 2022, and the Nifty fell from 18,604 to near 15,183 by June 2022, as you saw in Chapter 3.

body.title: What Does QT Do to Emerging Markets?
body.question: The Fed shrinks its balance sheet through QT while raising interest rates. What is the most likely effect on emerging markets like India?
options: More foreign money flows in because the US economy is slowing
Global liquidity tightens, the dollar strengthens and foreign investors tend to pull money out
No effect, because QT only affects the US bond market
Emerging market currencies strengthen as the Fed sells dollars
body.explanation: QT removes dollar liquidity from the global financial system and tends to push US yields up. Combined with rate hikes, it makes safe US assets more attractive and strengthens the dollar, so money flows out of riskier emerging markets. India's record FPI outflows in 2022 followed exactly this pattern.

children.text: Does the RBI Do QE?

Not in the Fed's sense. The RBI has bought government bonds in large amounts, including ₹2.2 lakh crore under G-SAP in 2021 and a record ₹6.39 lakh crore of OMO purchases in FY26. But the purpose and setting are different.

body.title: Fed QE vs RBI Bond Buying

columns.label: US Fed QE
points: Used when the policy rate is already near zero
Main aim: push long-term rates down to stimulate the economy
Trillions of dollars, sustained for years
Signals a deliberate expansion of the balance sheet

columns.label: RBI OMO purchases and G-SAP
points: Used with the repo rate well above zero, never below 4% even in 2020
Main aim: manage liquidity and keep the bond market orderly
Often offsets drains from forex intervention and currency demand
Can be reversed through OMO sales, as in September 2026

children.text: The 2026 Question: Will Warsh Shrink the Balance Sheet Again?

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has long argued that the Fed's balance sheet is too large and that QE distorted markets. Since taking over in May 2026, he has signalled he wants a smaller balance sheet over time, possibly coordinated with the US Treasury through a new accord on how much government debt the Fed holds. Analysts expect any move to be cautious, starting no earlier than late 2026, for example by continuing to run down mortgage securities while keeping Treasury holdings steady.

Not everyone agrees. Fed Governor Michael Barr has warned that shrinking the balance sheet is the wrong objective and could threaten financial stability. For India, the debate matters: renewed QT on top of rate hikes would mean tighter global liquidity and more pressure on emerging market flows.

body.title: Hikes Plus QT: What Would It Mean for India?
body.scenario: Suppose that later in 2026 the Fed, having started to raise rates, also announces a plan to gradually shrink its balance sheet again. US 10-year yields rise and the dollar strengthens. FPIs have already withdrawn a record ₹2.37 lakh crore from Indian equities this year, and the rupee is near 95 per dollar.
body.prompt: How could renewed QT affect Indian markets, and what could cushion the impact?
body.modelAnswer: Renewed QT would add a second source of tightening on top of rate hikes. It would drain dollar liquidity globally and likely push US long-term yields higher, narrowing the gap with Indian yields. That would encourage more FPI selling of Indian stocks and bonds, weigh on the rupee and push Indian G-Sec yields up, making it harder for the RBI to avoid hiking. Large-cap stocks with heavy foreign ownership, such as private banks, would be most exposed. Several things could cushion the impact. India's record forex reserves, above $785 billion after the FCNR(B) window, give the RBI firepower to smooth the rupee. Strong domestic flows, especially monthly SIP inflows of over ₹32,000 crore, can absorb foreign selling in equities. And if the Fed moves slowly and signals it clearly, markets have time to adjust, unlike the sudden shocks of 2013 and 2022.

body.title: Go Deeper: QE Around the World

children.text: The Fed was not alone. The Bank of Japan pioneered quantitative easing in the early 2000s and launched a far larger programme in 2013. The European Central Bank started large-scale government bond purchases in 2015, and the Bank of England ran its own programmes from 2009. At their peaks, several central banks owned a very large share of their own governments' bonds.

Because these programmes overlapped, their combined effect on global liquidity was enormous. You will look at the ECB and the Bank of Japan in more detail in the next lesson, including why Japan's exit from ultra-easy policy became a global market event.

The total assets a central bank holds. The Fed's peaked at $8.96 trillion in April 2022.

body.label: Federal Reserve H.4.1 Weekly Balance Sheet
body.description: The Fed publishes its full balance sheet every Thursday. Watching total assets tells you whether the Fed is adding liquidity to the world or pulling it back.

body.title: Watch Global Liquidity Like a Macro Investor
steps: Open the latest Fed H.4.1 release and note total assets compared with $6.7 trillion in early September 2026
Check whether the Fed's September 2026 statement mentioned any change to its balance sheet plans
Compare the latest monthly FPI equity flows into India with the record ₹2.74 lakh crore inflow of FY21
Track the US 10-year Treasury yield alongside the Nifty 50 for a month and note how often they move in opposite directions
Read one analyst note on a possible Fed-Treasury accord and think about what it would mean for emerging market flows

points: QE is large-scale bond buying with newly created reserves, used when policy rates are near zero; QT is its reversal.
The Fed's balance sheet grew from about $0.9 trillion before 2008 to a peak of $8.96 trillion in April 2022.
QT from June 2022 to December 2025 cut the balance sheet to about $6.57 trillion, reversing only about half of the pandemic expansion.
QE pushes investors into riskier assets and emerging markets; India received a record ₹2.74 lakh crore of FPI equity inflows in FY21.
QT and rate hikes reverse the flow: India saw record FPI equity outflows of ₹1.21 lakh crore in 2022.
The RBI's bond purchases manage liquidity rather than acting as QE, and Fed Chair Warsh's push for a smaller balance sheet is a key risk to watch for global liquidity.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. Balance sheet and flow figures are approximate and as reported up to mid-September 2026. Any future Fed balance sheet plans are subject to change.
